newsitem.title: PERU: South Korea's Kim meets Peru's President Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Kim meets Peru's President Fujimori.

text.p: South Korea's President Kim Young-sam and Peru's President Alberto Fujimori met on Friday and announced four accords aimed at strengthening trade links between the two Pacific Rim nations.

Fujimori said the agreements would offer Korean technical support for Peru's second largest industry, fishing, increase cooperation between their private sectors and establish a joint investigative operation in the Antarctic.

Kim was in Peru for three days on the last stop of a tour of five Latin American nations to pave the way for South Korean firms to expand into one of the region's fastest growing economies, projected at six percent a year to 2000.

He was accompanied by 42 businessmen including executives from the Hyundai, Sunkyong, Samsung and Daewoo groups, who were interested in investing in Peru, particularly the booming mining sector, Korean offficials said.
Fujimori said the investors had chosen a "magnificent moment" for their trip because Peru had a "new attitude to foreign capital."

"We regard investors from friendly nations like Korea as our allies in developing our economy," Fujimori said at the announcement of the accords. "We respond to the interest shown by the Korean investors as positively as possible so that we can do good business."

Fujimori, who wants Peru to emulate the Asian "tiger" nations, has steered the economy from chaos in 1990 when he took office to sustained growth thanks to free market policies that have encouraged outside investment.

Korean companies have skirted Latin America for years in favour of Europe, Asia and the Middle East. But as the region's economies emerge from a decade of debt and social unrest, a commercial assault from Seoul is seen as likely.

Prior to Kim's visit, the Hyundai group announced plans to invest $1.3 billion in Peru especially in mining. Trade between the two countries has soared 300 percent between 1990 and 1995 due to the exchange of South Korea's technology and capital for Peru's immense natural resources, Fujimori said.
Bilateral trade for 1996 is estimated to rise to $400 million, up from $317 million last year.

Kim, whose Latin American tour also took him to Guatemala, Chile, Argentina and Brazil, was to return home from Peru on Saturday morning. His visit to the region followed another high-profile tour from an Asian head-of state, Japan's Prime Minister Ryuatro Hashimoto, also to promote commercial links.
